title: About Me
text:
Hi! I’m currently a Master of City Planning student at the University of Pennsylvania, where I’m interested in the ways people and the environment interact. Before coming to Penn, I studied Environmental Science and Political Science at Villanova University, with a minor in Economics. My background has given me the opportunity to look at environmental and social issues from a few different perspectives, but GIS and spatial analysis have been what really helped bring those interests together.
Throughout my undergraduate research, I worked on projects involving wildfire vulnerability, climate change, coastal flooding, and environmental justice. I became interested in urban spatial analytics because I enjoy using data to understand why patterns occur in particular places and how those patterns affect different communities.
As I continue my studies at Penn, I hope to build on these skills and learn how spatial analytics can be used to address real planning challenges. I’m particularly interested in climate resilience, land use, and environmental equity, and I hope to eventually use spatial analysis to help cities make more informed and equitable planning decisions.

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
text:
The question
Every number the American Community Survey publishes is an estimate drawn from a sample, not a count. That means every number comes with a margin of error — a statement about how wrong it might be.
Most people ignore it. In this assignment, you won’t.
In this analysis, I look at total commuters across counties in California, and ask which communities we measure most and least reliably. Census data helps inform decisions about transporation and infrastructure, so differences in data reliability can affect how communities are represented in those decisions.

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
text:
Choosing what to measure

my_state <- "CA"        
my_variable <- "B08303_001"

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
text:
Pulling the data

county_data <- get_acs(
  geography = "county",
  variables = my_variable,
  state = my_state,
  year = 2023,
  survey = "acs5"
)

Let’s look at what came back.

dim(county_data)

[1] 58  5

head(county_data)

# A tibble: 6 × 5
  GEOID NAME                         variable   estimate   moe
  <chr> <chr>                        <chr>         <dbl> <dbl>
1 06001 Alameda County, California   B08303_001   636741  4570
2 06003 Alpine County, California    B08303_001      575   146
3 06005 Amador County, California    B08303_001    13424   667
4 06007 Butte County, California     B08303_001    80569  1671
5 06009 Calaveras County, California B08303_001    15129   785
6 06011 Colusa County, California    B08303_001     8670   606


California has 58 counties, which matches the 58 rows returned.

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
section: How big is the margin of error?
text:
How big is the margin of error?
A margin of error of 3,000 means something very different for an estimate of 20,000 than for an estimate of 200,000. To compare across places, we need it as a percentage.

county_data <- county_data %>%
  mutate(moe_pct = moe / estimate * 100)

Now sort to see which counties are measured least reliably.

county_data %>%
  arrange(desc(moe_pct)) %>%
  select(NAME, estimate, moe, moe_pct) %>%
  head(10)

# A tibble: 10 × 4
   NAME                        estimate   moe moe_pct
   <chr>                          <dbl> <dbl>   <dbl>
 1 Alpine County, California        575   146   25.4 
 2 Sierra County, California        921   167   18.1 
 3 Trinity County, California      3673   529   14.4 
 4 Modoc County, California        2732   282   10.3 
 5 Plumas County, California       6381   602    9.43
 6 Mono County, California         6305   457    7.25
 7 Colusa County, California       8670   606    6.99
 8 Mariposa County, California     6240   412    6.60
 9 Lake County, California        20228  1106    5.47
10 Lassen County, California       8730   477    5.46


Alpine County, California has the largest margin of error relative to its estimate, making it the least reliable county in the analysis. Its margin of error percentage is 25.4%.

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
text:
Sorting counties into reliability categories

county_data <- county_data %>%
  mutate(reliability = case_when(
    moe_pct < 3  ~ "High confidence",
    moe_pct < 8 ~ "Moderate",
    TRUE         ~ "Low confidence"
  ))

count(county_data, reliability)

# A tibble: 3 × 2
  reliability         n
  <chr>           <int>
1 High confidence    36
2 Low confidence      5
3 Moderate           17


I chose 3% and 8% as the cutoffs because they created a more useful spread of counties across the three reliability categories rather than putting almost every county into one group. The 3% cutoff represents relatively low uncertainty, while 8% identifies estimates with noticeably greater uncertainty. With these cutoffs, 36 counties are high confidence, 17 are moderate, and 5 are low confidence, making it easier to compare counties with different levels of reliability.

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
section: Is the margin of error bigger in small places?
text:
Is the margin of error bigger in small places?
To answer this we need population and our variable side by side, in the same row. That means a wide pull.

county_wide <- get_acs(
  geography = "county",
  variables = c(myvar = my_variable,
                pop   = "B01003_001"),
  state = my_state,
  year = 2023,
  survey = "acs5",
  output = "wide"
)

county_wide %>%
  select(NAME, myvarE, myvarM, popE) %>%
  head(10)

# A tibble: 10 × 4
   NAME                            myvarE myvarM    popE
   <chr>                            <dbl>  <dbl>   <dbl>
 1 Alameda County, California      636741   4570 1651949
 2 Alpine County, California          575    146    1695
 3 Amador County, California        13424    667   41029
 4 Butte County, California         80569   1671  209470
 5 Calaveras County, California     15129    785   45995
 6 Colusa County, California         8670    606   21895
 7 Contra Costa County, California 448235   4119 1161458
 8 Del Norte County, California      9273    461   27293
 9 El Dorado County, California     69437   1669  192299
10 Fresno County, California       374166   3296 1012152



county_wide <- county_wide %>%
  mutate(moe_pct = myvarM / myvarE * 100) %>%
  mutate(reliability = case_when(
    moe_pct < 3  ~ "High confidence",
    moe_pct < 8 ~ "Moderate",
    TRUE         ~ "Low confidence"
  ))

Now compare the average population of counties in each reliability category.

county_wide %>%
  group_by(reliability) %>%
  summarize(
    n_counties = n(),
    avg_population = mean(popE)
  )

# A tibble: 3 × 3
  reliability     n_counties avg_population
  <chr>                <int>          <dbl>
1 High confidence         36       1065959.
2 Low confidence           5          9713 
3 Moderate                17         48218 


The results have a strong relationship between county population and the reliability of the estimates. High-confidence counties have an average population of 1,065,959, compared with only 48,218 for moderate-confidence counties, and 9,713 for low-confidence counties. Smaller communities tend to have greater uncertainty in their estimates because fewer people are represented in the survey sample.

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
text:
What this means for policy
The counties with the least reliable commuter estimates are concentrated among California’s smaller, more rural communities. Alpine County has the highest relative margin of error, with an estimated 575 commuters and a margin of error of 146, or 25.4% of its estimate. Sierra County has only 921 estimated commuters and an MOE of 167, giving it an 18.1% margin of error. Trinity County also has substantial uncertainty, with 3,673 commuters and a 14.4% margin of error, while Modoc and Plumas counties have margins of error of 10.3% and 9.43%, respectively. This is very different from a large county like Los Angeles, which has nearly 4 million estimated commuters but a relative margin of error of only 0.31%. The difference reflects how the ACS is based on a sample rather than a complete count of every household. Smaller counties have fewer sampled households representing their communities, so their estimates can be less precise. This creates a potential problem when Census data is used for transportation planning or infrastructure funding. If a state agency treated every county’s commuter estimate as equally certain, it could make decisions based on differences that are partly the result of sampling uncertainty. For example, Alpine County’s estimate of 575 could be substantially higher or lower than its true value. Rural counties such as Alpine, Sierra, and Trinity could therefore have their transportation needs underestimated or overestimated when compared with larger counties whose estimates are much more precise.

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
section: Optional challenges - For those craving more
text:
Optional challenges - For those craving more






NoteDelete this box



None of these are graded. There are no extra points. A complete, well-written assignment earns a 2 either way.
They’re here for anyone who finished the above and found it straightforward. Pick one (or more) that interests you.

Propagate the margin of error. If you compute a derived value — a percentage, a ratio, a sum — its uncertainty depends on the uncertainty of its inputs, and you can’t just carry the original MOE along. The Census Bureau publishes formulas for this, and tidycensus implements them: moe_sum(), moe_prop(), moe_ratio(). Compute something derived, and get its margin of error right.
Parameterize the report. Add params: to the YAML so the state is an input rather than hard-coded, and the same file regenerates for any state. Render it from the terminal with quarto render assignment2.qmd -P state:NY.
Write a function and iterate. Wrap the data pull in a function, then use purrr::map_dfr() to run it across several states at once. Does the small-places-are-noisier pattern hold everywhere, or are some states different?
Change the geographic scale. Run the same variable at geography = "tract" inside one county. Compare the margins of error to what you saw at county level. What does that imply about the resolution at which you can actually trust ACS data?

If you try one, add a short section describing what you did and what you found.

title: Verify the Claim: Poverty Change in Philadelphia Neighborhoods
text: Article analyzed: Lubrano, Alfred. “New Census figures on Philly neighborhoods show inequality, high numbers of whites living in poverty.” WHYY / Philadelphia Inquirer, December 6, 2018. https://whyy.org/articles/new-census-figures-on-philly-neighborhoods-show-inequality-high-numbers-of-whites-living-in-poverty/

title: Verify the Claim: Poverty Change in Philadelphia Neighborhoods
text:
Part 1: Reconstruct
The article reports neighborhood poverty rates without naming its source table, so I reconstructed them using the standard ACS poverty table, B17001 (“Poverty Status in the Past 12 Months by Sex by Age”). The poverty rate for each tract is the number of people below the poverty level (B17001_002) divided by the number of people for where poverty status is determined (B17001_001). I used that second variable as the denominator rather than total population because the Census Bureau does not assess poverty for everyone. People living in group quarters such as college dorms, prisons, or nursing homes are excluded, so dividing by total population would be an understatement. I used the ACS 5-year estimates (acs5) for 2006–2010 (year = 2010) and 2013–2017 (year = 2017), the two periods the article compares. The 5-year survey is the only option at this scale: the 1-year ACS is not published for areas under 65,000 people, which includes every census tract.
The article does not state which table it used, so I assume B17001, the Bureau’s standard poverty measure. More importantly, the article reports figures for named neighborhoods like Fairhill and Eastwick, which are not Census geographies, and it does not publish which tracts it combined to build them. I worked at the tract level, so my figures will not match the article’s exactly. Both periods use 2010 census tract boundaries, so each tract refers to the same area in both years. The two periods do not overlap because the first ends in 2010 and the second begins in 2013. That means they are independent samples, and a difference between them can be tested statistically. Each estimate is an average of five years of data, so the comparison describes the difference between two five-year averages, roughly centered on 2008 and 2015, instead than a change between two exact years.


Show code
# Week 3 get_poverty() function
get_poverty <- function(yr) {
  get_acs(
    geography = "tract",
    state     = "PA",
    county    = "Philadelphia",
    variables = c(below_poverty = "B17001_002",
                  total         = "B17001_001"),
    year      = yr,
    survey    = "acs5",
    output    = "wide"
  ) %>%
    mutate(
      share     = below_povertyE / totalE,
      # A rate is a proportion, so its MOE comes from moe_prop(),
      # not from the count's MOE
      share_moe = moe_prop(below_povertyE, totalE,
                           below_povertyM, totalM),
      period    = paste0(yr - 4, "-", yr)
    )
}

poverty_raw <- bind_rows(
  get_poverty(2010),
  get_poverty(2017)
)

title: Verify the Claim: Poverty Change in Philadelphia Neighborhoods
text:
Part 2: Test

[WRITE: Fifteen tract-years came back with no poverty rate, and every one of them had zero people in the poverty universe, so the rate is 0 divided by 0, which doe snot give us a real number. These are places where basically nobody lives, like parks, the airport, or industrial areas, so there’s no poverty rate to measure. I removed them before calculating reliability and change, since leaving them in would add blanks without telling us anything about where people actually live.]


Show code
# Same filter(total_popE > 0) 
poverty <- poverty_raw %>%
  filter(totalE > 0) %>%
  mutate(
    # CV
    cv = (share_moe / 1.645) / share * 100,
    reliability = case_when(
      share == 0 ~ "Undefined (rate is 0)",   # CV would divide by zero
      cv < 12    ~ "Reliable",
      cv <= 40   ~ "Somewhat reliable",
      TRUE       ~ "Unreliable"
    )
  )

poverty %>%
  count(period, reliability)


# A tibble: 7 × 3
  period    reliability               n
  <chr>     <chr>                 <int>
1 2006-2010 Reliable                 11
2 2006-2010 Somewhat reliable       321
3 2006-2010 Undefined (rate is 0)     2
4 2006-2010 Unreliable               43

Reliability table


Show code
poverty %>%
  filter(period == "2013-2017", share > 0) %>%
  mutate(
    dot = case_when(
      cv < 12  ~ "🟢",
      cv <= 40 ~ "🟡",
      TRUE     ~ "🔴"
    ),
    tract = str_remove(NAME, ", Philadelphia County, Pennsylvania")
  ) %>%
  arrange(desc(cv)) %>%
  slice_head(n = 20) %>%
  select(dot, tract, share, share_moe, cv, reliability) %>%
  gt() %>%
  fmt_percent(columns = c(share, share_moe), decimals = 1) %>%
  fmt_number(columns = cv, decimals = 1) %>%
  cols_label(
    dot         = "",
    tract       = "Tract",

Change and significance


Show code
# Put the two periods side by side 
# Keep only GEOID as the ID so tracts match even if NAME text differs by year
poverty_wide <- poverty %>%
  select(GEOID, period, share, share_moe) %>%
  pivot_wider(
    names_from  = period,
    values_from = c(share, share_moe)
  )

nrow(poverty_wide)   


[1] 377


Show code
# Same z-test but applied to rates instead of counts
poverty_tested <- poverty_wide %>%
  filter(!is.na(`share_2006-2010`), !is.na(`share_2013-2017`)) %>%
  mutate(
    change   = `share_2013-2017` - `share_2006-2010`,
    se_1     = `share_moe_2006-2010` / 1.645,
    se_2     = `share_moe_2013-2017` / 1.645,
    se_diff  = sqrt(se_1^2 + se_2^2),
    moe_diff = se_diff * 1.645,
    z        = change / se_diff,
    significant = abs(z) > 1.645,       # 90% confidence
    result = case_when(
      !significant ~ "No detectable change",
      change > 0   ~ "Detectable increase",
      TRUE         ~ "Detectable decrease"
    )
  )

poverty_tested %>%
  count(result)

  <chr>                <int>
1 Detectable decrease     27
2 Detectable increase     36
3 No detectable change   313


Only 63 of 376 tracts (about 17%) had a poverty rate change big enough to be real (not plagued by survey noise): 36 went up and 27 went down. The other 313 tracts (about 83%) showed no detectable change.


Error bar chart

  geom_point() +

                    ymax = change + moe_diff), width = 0.3) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  coord_flip() +
  theme_minimal() +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +

    color    = "Significant at 90%?"
  )









Even among the 25 biggest apparent changes, 4 have error bars that cross zero, so we cannot say those changes are real. Tract 989100 is the extreme case because its margin of error runs from about −200 to +245 percentage points, which is wider than a poverty rate can even move.

title: Verify the Claim: Poverty Change in Philadelphia Neighborhoods
text:
Part 3: Adjudicate
The article’s biggest-picture claim holds up narrowly. Some parts of Philadelphia did become poorer between 2006–2010 and 2013–2017. Thirty-six tracts show a poverty increase big enough to rule out survey noise, so the idea that poverty jumped in certain places is supported. But the article’s overall story, that poverty kept rising “robustly” across the city after the recession, is not supported. Most tracts (313 of 376, or 83%) show no detectable change at all, and detectable decreases (27 tracts) were almost as common as detectable increases (36). The ranking claims did not hold true either. Calling Eastwick’s jump from 12% to 26% the “greatest increase of any community” treats estimates like exact numbers. Shown by the error bar chart, even the biggest apparent changes have wide, overlapping margins of error, so there is no way to say which place changed the most.
A lot of the article’s claims cannot even be determined from my analysis. The neighborhood numbers for Fairhill (61% poverty), Eastwick, Holmesburg, and Mayfair depend on tract groupings the article never published, so I could not recreate them exactly. The white poverty claims, including the headline, the 22 majority-white neighborhoods where poverty rose, and Holmesburg going from 2% to 19%, would need the race-specific poverty tables (B17001A–I). The citywide white poverty jump from 14.8% to 19.4% comes from the 1-year ACS, which is a different survey than the more relibale 5-year estimates I used. And the Tioga-Nicetown income drop is about median household income, a whole different variable. Neighborhoods starting at 1–2% poverty, like Holmesburg and Mayfair, probably had really shaky baseline estimates, which makes those dramatic jumps even harder to trust without seeing the margins of error.

title: Verify the Claim: Poverty Change in Philadelphia Neighborhoods
text:
Part 4: Rewrite
Philadelphia’s poverty problem did not spread across the whole city after the Great Recession. It dug in deeper in specific places. New federal survey data comparing 2006–2010 with 2013–2017 show that poverty clearly rose in 36 of the city’s 376 census tracts, while it clearly fell in 27. Across most of Philadelphia, the numbers barely moved once you account for the survey’s margin of error. That still leaves a city where roughly one in four people lives in poverty, and pockets like Fairhill where the need is overwhelming. But the survey can’t settle which neighborhood got hit hardest, and dramatic jumps in places with small populations may say more about sampling than about real change.
